content.text: Gen ANESTHETICS & PERIOPERATIVE meds
MOA of gen anesthetics: directly activate GABA-A receptors
Inhalation anesthetics:
Volatile Anesthetics – halothane, isoflurane, desflurane
Gaseous Anesthetics – nitrous oxide
Organ system effects of inhaled anesthetics:
CNS: ↑cerebral blood flow
Cardiovasc: decreases MAP & contractility → reduces myocard O2 consumption
Resp: bronchodilation effects (caution in asthma/COPD), resp depression
Nitrous Oxide – clin uses:
Prod analgesia and amnesia in dental procedures where it may be used alone; when used alone, only Stage II can be achieved, and ⍉skeletal musc paralysis = achieved

Adjuvant to supp the actions of other inhaled anesthetics; administering nitrous oxide @ inspired concentrations of 50-70% together w another volatile anesthetic decreases the dose requirement of the volatile agent w a reduction of its undesirable side effects
Rapid induction for surg procedures: poor blood solubility results in rapid tissue uptake
smooth transition from awake to anesthetized state
decreases irritate from volatile agents

↓tissue solubility results in less tissue accum during prolonged procedures and rapid elim from the lungs after d/c; often used to maintain anesthesia near the end of a procedure during elim of the volatile anesthetic, allowing rapid emergence once surg = completed
Halothane – clin uses:
Rapid, smooth induction of anesthesia, esp when administered w 60-70% nitrous oxide
Maintenance of anesthesia in children (commonly used in pediatric practice); infrequently used in adults (replaced by a newer volatile agent after induction = achieved)
WARNINGS: idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity – acute post-op hepatitis
Desflurane – clin uses:
⍉suitable for induction:  ↑incidence of resp irritate (coughing, breath-holding, apnea, ↑secretions, laryngospasms); use IV agent for induction b4 desflurane anesthesia
Sevoflurane – clin uses:
One of the most commonly used agents since its introduction
May be used for rapid inhalational induction which = USU well tolerated; nonpungent and lowest amount of airway irritate
Major use = for maintenance
IV Anesthetic Agents:
Used to facilitate rapid induction of anesthesia; have replaced inhalation agents as the preferred method of anesthesia induction in most settings except for pediatric anesthesia
Also commonly used to provide sedation during monitored anesthesia care and for pts in ICU settings
Benzodiazepines – desirable pharm actions:
anterograde amnesia
absence of retrograde amnesia
minimal cardiopulm depression
Anticonvuls effects (lorazepam and diazepam are used in tx of status epilepticus)
relatively safe in OD ← availability of a specific benzodiazepine antagonist (flumazenil, Romazicon®)
Benzodiazepines – uses:
Pre-op med: sedation, amnesia
IV conscious sedation
: midazolam
Suppress sz activity: status epilepticus
Opioids – clin uses in anesthesia: fentanyl (Sublimaze®), sufentanil (Sufenta®), alfentanil (Alfenta®), remifentanil
Perioperative analgesia
Supp of inhaled anesthetics for maintenance
Induction and maintenance:  use of lrg doses of opioids to achieve gen anesthesia in pts undergoing ♡ surg or major surg where circulatory reserve = minimal
droperidol/fentanyl (Innovar®, C-II):
Combo of droperidol (Inapsine®), an antipsych (
neuroleptic
) agent, and fentanyl (Sublimaze®), an
opiate anesthetic/analgesic
A state of "neuroleptic analgesia" = produced where the pt = psychologically indifferent to the environment and free from pain, but may still be conscious
This = desirable for endoscopic procedures where some degree of pt cooperation = needed
Remifentanil (Ultiva):
Opioid agonist @ mu receptors.
Indicated for use as an analgesic agent during induction and maintenance of gen anesthesia for inpt and outpt procedures
Also indicated for use as an analgesic component of monitored anesthesia care
Etomidate (Amidate)
Short-acting hypnotic; GABA-like effects
Very rapid induction (LOC in < 30 seconds) and recovery (w.in 3 min)
→ minimal CV and resp depressant effects (slight hypotension, ⍉Δ in HR, ↓incidence of apnea)
⍉analgesia
SE: N/V, pain on inj, myoclonus; may also cause adrenocortical suppression
Ketamine
; C-III:
Synthetic nonbarbiturate anesthetic, PCP derivative
Major actions are thru inhibition of the NMDA-r complex
→ a state of "dissociative anesthesia" characterized by catatonia (sedation, immobility, eyes remain open w a slow nystagmic gaze), amnesia, and analgesia.
The pt feels dissociated and detached from the environment (advantageous for burn dressing chgs).
Induction = rapid (LOC w.in 30 sec) and analgesia/amnesia = good, but musc relaxation = poor.
Cardiovasc stim = marked and results in ↑BP and HR.
Recovery = slow and = often marked by disorientation, disturbing dreams, hallucinations, and sensory and perceptual illusions (emergence “delirium” rxns)
IV diazepam given 5 min b4 ketamine may reduce the incidence of these "emergence" effects.
It may be useful in poor-risk geriatric pts and shock pts ← its cardio stimulatory properties; also used in painful procedures in children.
Propofol
Approved 1989 for induction and maintenance of gen anesthesia and in 1993 for sedation of adult pts receiving mech ventilation
Used as a component of balanced anesthesia (cont infusion for maintenance plus an opioid or inhaled agent) and as anesthetic for outpt procedures (“day surgery”)
Also used for sedation in the ICU as well as conscious sedation and short-duration gen anesthesia in locations outside the operating room
approved for sedation in pediatric pts; most serious comp =
propofol infusion syndrome
initially described in children receiving the drug
Dexmedetomidine (Precedex)
Relatively selective alpha-2-r agonist; IV sedative
Clin Use:
for use in ICU to sedate pts who are initially intubated and mechanically ventilated
sedation prior to and/or during surg or other procedures of nonintubated pts
SE: hypotension, brady, nausea
Induction using IV anesthetics:
Propofol – DOC for outpt undergoing ambulatory surg
Benzodiazepines
Diazepam and lorazepam are rarely used for induction ← slow onset times, ↑variability of dose-response, and prolonged residual effects (slow hepatic clearance)
Midazolam has faster onset and may be used for induction in some cases, but its slow elim USU → excessively slow recovery and longer cog impairment than other agents
Used as a co-induction agent w other IV agents; lessens the CV effects and emergence rxns of ketamine
Use of ketamine or etomidate for induction = restricted to cases where their actions offer advantages over other IV agents
Etomidate can facilitate BP stabilization in pts w severe Hdz or unstable angina
Perioperative meds
BDZs: prod mild sedation w amnesia; lorazepam
Short- or intermediate-acting barbiturates
Ordered hs b4 surg for sedation/sleep
Secobarbital (Seconal®); infrequently used
First-generation antihist
Prod sedation as side effect
Promethazine (Phenergan®); also potentiates analgesia
Hydroxyzine (Vistaril®, Atarax®), diphenhydramine (Benadryl®)
Antipsych
Side effects:  sedative, anticholinergic, antiemetic effects
Droperidol (Inapsine®), quetiapine (Seroquel®)
Analgesia – preanesthetic analgesia w/ opioid analgesics:
Morphine, meperidine
May decrease amount of gen anesthetic required
May prolong recovery, and cause N/V, constipation, and urinary retention
Fentanyl transmucosal system
Indicated as a preanesthetic med in children/adults and for conscious sedation prior to diagnostic or therapeutic procedures
Boxed warning:  risk of hypovent, requires close monitoring
Contraindications: children < 15 kg, or for tx of acute or chronic pain
Antiemetics
Prev & tx of post-op N/V –
ondansetron, granisetron HCl
Droperidol (Inapsine®)
Indicated for prev and tx of N/V
Lower doses effective for prophylaxis of N/V than are used for antipsych effect; higher doses (> 1.25 mg) cause ↑drowsiness
SE:
sedation
, hypotension; extrapyramidal Sx rare
Boxed warning:
QT prolongation and prod of torsades
; monitor EKG b4 and 2-3 hrs after administration
Prochlorperazine (Compazine®):
Substantiated effect in tx of post-op N/V; less evidence for preventive role
SE: sedation, extrapyramidal rxns
Metoclopramide (Reglan®):
Unlabeled use for post-op N/V; relatively weak antiemetic for PONV ; higher doses may be more effective; administer IV over ± 1-2 min near end of surg
Lower incidence of sedation and extrapyramidal rxns compared to droperidol
Promethazine (Phenergan®):
IV/IM only; SC route contraindicated
effective for prophylaxis and tx of post-op N/V
use of promethazine = limited by its sedative action
Scopolamine
Transdermal scopolamine = applied 2-4 hrs prior to surg for prev of N/V assoc w recovery from anesthesia and surg
SE: dry mouth, mydriasis, drowsiness; confusion or agitation may occur, esp in older adults w baseline cog impairment
Scopolamine patch = contraindicated in pts w angle closure glaucoma
Neuromusc BLOCKING AGENTS (NMBAs)
NMBAs – clin uses:
Perioperative: adjunct to gen anesthesia to facilitate endotracheal intubation and to relax skeletal musc during surg
NMBAs are never used as substitutes for safe and adequate levels of gen anesthesia; NMBAs have ⍉effects on consciousness or pain threshold
ICU: paralysis of mechanically ventilated pts in ICUs; NMBAs are never used in ICUs w.o adequate sedation and analgesia
Control of musc spasms assoc w certain dz states, ex, tetanus, status epilepticus
Decrease the musc activity resulting from ECT
NMBAs – MOA: interfere w/ neurotransmission by:
Occupying and activating the nicotinic-r for a prolonged period of time, leading to blockade, which occurs w the
depolarizing
agents; or
Competitively antagonizing the actions of ACh @ nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, which occurs w the
nondepolarizing
agents.
